summary: This document consolidates the iSCSI protocol, a transport for SCSI that runs over TCP and aims to comply with SCSI Architecture Model SAM-2. RFC 3720 defined the original protocol, and later RFCs, including 3721 and 3980, added to it. This document brings it together in one place.

plainLanguage.summary: SCSI is a set of commands for storage devices. iSCSI carries those commands over TCP connections, so an initiator can communicate with a target across an IP network. The RFC defines how the parties identify each other, set up a session, exchange data, recover from errors, and protect access.

questions: what is an iscsi qualified name
subtitle: How iSCSI carries SCSI storage commands over TCP/IP, with rules for setup, data transfer, recovery, and security.

tldr.problem: SCSI provides commands for storage and other I/O devices, but its earlier transports were designed for specific I/O connections and had limited distance. This RFC specifies how to carry SCSI over TCP/IP.
tldr.mechanism: An initiator sends SCSI commands to a target inside iSCSI Protocol Data Units over one or more TCP connections. Login authenticates the parties and negotiates parameters before command traffic begins; the session groups the connections and coordinates their commands.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7143 consolidates and supersedes RFCs 3720, 3980, 4850, and 5048, and updates RFC 3721. Its text governs where its meaning differs from those earlier RFCs.

today: RFC 7143 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3720, RFC 3980, RFC 4850, and RFC 5048, and updates RFC 3721; the RFC says its meaning supersedes those earlier documents where they differ.

sections.title: Why iSCSI Carries SCSI over TCP/IP
sections.content:
The Small Computer System Interface (SCSI) is a family of protocols for requesting work from I/O devices, especially storage. A client called an initiator sends commands to a server called a target; the target contains one or more logical units, such as storage devices. A SCSI transport carries those commands between the two sides.

Earlier SCSI transports included Parallel SCSI, IPI, IEEE 1394, and Fibre Channel. The RFC describes them as I/O-specific and limited in distance. iSCSI carries SCSI packets over TCP/IP so the protocol can use existing Internet infrastructure and management facilities.

RFC 7143 consolidates earlier iSCSI specifications and makes additional updates. It aims to comply with the SCSI Architecture Model, which defines the architecture shared by SCSI protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: iSCSI carries storage commands from an initiator to a target over TCP/IP. It gives SCSI a transport that can use IP networks instead of only I/O-specific connections.

sections.title: How Sessions Group TCP Connections
sections.content:
The SCSI layer creates and receives SCSI Command Descriptor Blocks, which contain command details. The iSCSI layer puts these commands and related information into Protocol Data Units (PDUs), the messages exchanged by iSCSI, and carries them over TCP connections.

One or more TCP connections between an initiator and a target form an iSCSI session. Each connection has a connection ID. The sides treat all connections in one session as access to the same target and initiator. A session supports at least one connection; an implementation may support several.

iSCSI numbers commands across the whole session so the target can deliver them in order, even when the session has several connections. Status numbers are tracked per connection, while data sequence numbers help detect missing data or transfer requests. Each command's responses and related data use the connection that carried the command, unless recovery explicitly assigns the command to another connection.
sections.plainLanguage:
The SCSI layer creates storage commands, and the iSCSI layer packages them into messages for TCP connections. A session groups those connections so the parties can treat them as one relationship and keep commands in order.

Each command normally gets its reply and data on the same connection that carried the command. The protocol can move a command to another connection during recovery.

sections.title: Names, Network Portals, and Discovery
sections.content:
Every iSCSI node must have an iSCSI name. The name identifies a logical initiator or target, not a network adapter or address. Names are globally unique and permanent, so a node can move or use several addresses without changing its name. Implementations must accept names up to 223 bytes.

The RFC defines three name formats: iqn., based on a registered domain name and date; eui., based on an IEEE EUI-64 identifier; and naa., based on a Network Address Authority identifier. Names use UTF-8 and Normalization Form C; uppercase characters are prohibited.

A Network Portal is a TCP/IP address used to reach an iSCSI node. A target portal also has a listening TCP port. Initiators can discover target names and addresses with the SendTargets text request. Equipment needing broader discovery capabilities should implement iSNS; the RFC says implementations should not rely on SLP-based discovery.
sections.plainLanguage:
An iSCSI name identifies a logical node and stays the same when its network address changes. The address used to reach it is called a Network Portal.

An initiator can ask a target for available target names and addresses with SendTargets. The RFC recommends iSNS for broader discovery and says not to rely on SLP-based discovery.

sections.title: The PDU and Its Basic Header
sections.content:
Every iSCSI message is a PDU. Each begins with a fixed 48-byte Basic Header Segment (BHS). The header identifies the PDU type and data length; when used, it also carries a Logical Unit Number and an Initiator Task Tag. The task tag identifies a task throughout the session.

A PDU may also contain Additional Header Segments, a header digest, a data segment, and a data digest. The header digest checks the header; the data digest checks the data. The parties negotiate whether to use digests during login. The default for both digest keys is None, while every initiator and target must implement CRC32C for digest checking.

Segments are padded to a four-byte boundary, and padding should be zero. The data length field counts payload bytes but excludes padding and digests. PDU opcodes distinguish messages such as SCSI Command, SCSI Response, Data-In, Data-Out, Ready To Transfer (R2T), Login, and Logout.
sections.plainLanguage:
Every iSCSI message starts with a 48-byte header. It tells the receiver what kind of message follows and how much data it carries.

Optional header and data checks can help detect errors. The sender and receiver agree during login whether to use them.

sections.title: Commands, Reads, and Writes
sections.content:
After login, the initiator sends a SCSI Command PDU for an operation. Its fields include the command, the logical unit, a task tag, and the expected data length. A read sends data from the target in Data-In PDUs. A write sends data from the initiator in Data-Out PDUs. The target returns a response with the operation's status.

For a write, the target can request data with an R2T PDU. The R2T specifies the requested buffer offset and length; the initiator returns the data in Data-Out PDUs. The initiator may also send a limited first burst without waiting for an R2T. It can put immediate data in the command PDU or send unsolicited Data-Out PDUs, subject to negotiated settings and the FirstBurstLength limit.

Task tags associate data with commands, and data sequence numbers let the parties detect missing data or R2T messages. A command's response and data remain on its original TCP connection unless the parties explicitly reassign its connection allegiance during recovery.
sections.plainLanguage:
A read command asks the target to send data; a write command sends data to the target. The target returns a status when the command finishes.

For a write, the target can first send an R2T message that says which data it is ready to receive. The parties can also agree to let the initiator send a limited amount of data before that request.

sections.title: Login and Parameter Negotiation
sections.content:
Login prepares a TCP connection for iSCSI, authenticates the parties, negotiates security and operating parameters, and creates a session or joins an existing one. Before login succeeds, the connection carries only Login Requests and Login Responses. Once the connection reaches the Full Feature Phase, the initiator can send SCSI commands.

Login has a security negotiation stage and an operational parameter negotiation stage. If both are used, security comes first. The parties exchange parameters as UTF-8 key=value text. Some keys declare a value; others let one side propose choices and the other select a supported value. A negotiation takes effect as one unit after it succeeds.

Some operational parameters can also be negotiated later with Text Requests and Responses. Examples set the maximum data segment size, the amount of data in a burst, and the error recovery level. The parties use the lower of their proposed recovery levels.
sections.plainLanguage:
Login sets up the connection before the initiator can send storage commands. The parties can authenticate each other and agree on settings during this exchange.

They send settings as named values in text messages. Some settings are proposals that the other side accepts or changes.

sections.title: Error Handling and Recovery
sections.content:
Recovery addresses errors such as a PDU that fails its digest check and a TCP connection that stops working. The RFC defines four recovery scopes: recovery within a command, within a connection, recovery of a connection, and recovery of a whole session. An implementation can support different recovery capabilities as long as the behavior seen by its peer remains interoperable.

The parties negotiate an ErrorRecoveryLevel. Level 0 provides session recovery and must be supported. Level 1 adds recovery for digest failures. Level 2 adds connection recovery, including the ability to reassign an active command to another connection when supported. Each higher level includes the lower levels, and the session uses the lower value negotiated by the two sides.

For example, an initiator can ask for a missing status or data PDU with a SNACK request. After a connection failure, it can log out the failed connection and use TASK REASSIGN to continue a command on another connection if the target supports that capability. Session recovery closes all connections and starts a new session.
sections.plainLanguage:
iSCSI can respond to an error by recovering one command, a connection, or the whole session. The negotiated recovery level sets which methods both sides can use.

When a connection fails, a supported recovery method can move an unfinished command to another connection. If recovery cannot continue, the parties can start a new session.

sections.title: Authentication and Packet Protection
sections.content:
Storage commands sent over IP need protection against false identities, changed or replayed messages, and eavesdropping. The RFC provides two complementary mechanisms: authentication during iSCSI login and packet protection with IPsec. Implementations must support both mechanisms; use of in-band authentication is strongly recommended, while use of IPsec is optional.

The authentication methods include Kerberos, Secure Remote Password (SRP), Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP), and None. Every initiator and target must implement CHAP, while the other listed methods are optional. Methods that use cleartext passwords must not be used. Authentication alone does not encrypt later traffic: without IPsec, PDUs after login travel in the clear.

CHAP can be vulnerable to offline password guessing when used without encryption. The RFC requires support for randomly generated CHAP secrets up to 128 bits. If a secret has fewer than 96 random bits, IPsec encryption must be enforced. The RFC also requires initiators and targets to use different CHAP secrets for authentication in opposite directions.
sections.plainLanguage:
Login authentication checks who is connecting, while IPsec can protect packets as they travel. The RFC recommends authentication and makes IPsec support a requirement for implementations, although using IPsec is optional.

Without IPsec, messages after login are not encrypted. The RFC warns that weak CHAP secrets need IPsec protection.

sections.title: What This Consolidated Edition Changes
sections.content:
RFC 7143 brings RFCs 3720, 3980, 4850, and 5048 together and updates RFC 3721. It states that this edition supersedes the earlier documents wherever their meanings differ.

The changes include removing marker negotiation and SPKM authentication, changing FastAbort from a mandatory requirement to a recommendation, and requiring support for IPsec v2 while recommending IPsec v3. The RFC also adds Kerberos security guidance, clarifies discovery behavior, and changes how iSCSI extension names are registered.

RFC 7143 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. Its listed metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.
sections.plainLanguage:
This RFC gathers earlier iSCSI rules into one specification and revises some of them. When it disagrees with an earlier specification, this RFC takes precedence.

It is a Proposed Standard from April 2014. It obsoletes four earlier RFCs and updates RFC 3721.

fields.name: Reserved, I bit, Opcode
fields.desc: The opcode identifies the PDU type; I marks immediate delivery on a request.

fields.name: F bit and opcode-specific fields
fields.desc: F marks the final or only PDU of a sequence; other bits depend on the opcode.

fields.name: TotalAHSLength
fields.desc: Total length of additional header segments, in four-byte words.

fields.name: DataSegmentLength
fields.desc: Data payload length in bytes, excluding padding.

fields.name: LUN or opcode-specific fields
fields.desc: Identifies a logical unit when the opcode uses one.

fields.name: Initiator Task Tag
fields.desc: Identifies the task across the session.

fields.name: Opcode-specific fields
fields.desc: The meaning of these fields depends on the PDU opcode.
